sections.h2: Where is Naperville and what does that mean for a seller?
sections.html:
Naperville is a city about 28 miles west of Chicago on the DuPage River, and it sits in two counties, DuPage and Will. The Census Bureau puts the July 1, 2025 estimate at 153,114 residents, up 2.4% from the April 2020 base, on roughly 39 square miles of land.

The settlement began in 1831 as Naper's Settlement, became a village in 1857 and was reincorporated as a city in 1890. It served as the DuPage County seat from 1839 until Wheaton took that role in 1868. Growth then came in a rush: the census counted 12,933 people in 1960, 85,351 in 1990 and 128,358 in 2000. A house here can therefore be a downtown property older than that boom or a subdivision home from the 1980s and 1990s, and buyers and appraisers treat those two groups differently.

The city spreads across six townships. Winfield, Milton, Naperville and Lisle are on the DuPage side, while Wheatland and DuPage townships are on the Will side. Several enclaves are cut out of the city limits, including the unincorporated Tamarack neighborhood in the southwest, so a Naperville mailing address does not always mean the property is inside city limits.

sections.h2: Which county records a Naperville deed, DuPage or Will?
sections.html:
It depends on which side of the county line the parcel is on, and your tax bill or your last recorded deed shows the county. DuPage parcels go to the DuPage County Recorder, and Will parcels go to the Will County Recorder of Deeds in Joliet.

The two offices publish different fee schedules for the same kind of document:

OfficeStandard deed or document feeWhat the schedule says it includes
DuPage County Recorder$86.00Recording, document storage ($10), GIS ($31), real property ($1) and Rental Housing Support Program ($18)
Will County Recorder of Deeds$90.00 (effective October 1, 2025)A $19.00 Rental Housing Support Program surcharge, which is dropped for government filers

Sources: the DuPage County Recorder forms and fee schedules page and the Will County Recorder fee notice effective October 1, 2025. The DuPage page states that its fees can change without notice, so ask the recorder for the current figure before closing.

For questions about the state transfer declaration, the DuPage page points filers to the Illinois Department of Revenue MyDec help line at 844-445-1114. On the Will side, the recorder's guidelines list what a deed needs: preparer and return addresses, the permanent index number, a legal description, a notarized original deed, the grantee name and address, a tax bill name and address, and a completed transfer declaration or exemption.

sections.h2: How does Naperville's real estate transfer tax stamp work?
sections.html:
Under the city ordinance, the buyer of a residential or commercial property inside incorporated Naperville buys the transfer tax stamp. The city's page prints the rate as $1.50 per $500 of purchase price, rounded up to the next $500 step.

The stamp applies only to incorporated property. The city points owners to its Your Place application, under Planning/Zoning Info, to check whether an address is inside the limits. The Will County Recorder's deed checklist also names Naperville among the municipalities whose transfer stamps must be on a deed.

The paperwork the city lists for a stamp is short:

  • A Statement of Open Account letter, requested online no later than seven business days before closing.
  • A sales contract, a PTAX (MyDec) form or a sheriff's receipt that carries both buyer and seller signatures.
  • A copy of the deed that will be recorded with the county.

Plan for up to seven business days of processing whether you apply online or drop a packet at the Finance Department. The Customer Care Center at 630-420-6059 answers questions Monday through Friday, 7 am to 7 pm. Because the open account statement has its own seven business day lead time, a closing date set only a week out leaves no slack.

sections.h2: When does a Naperville deed need an exempt stamp instead?
sections.html:
An exempt stamp is required when a deed changes on property you already own and no sale price is involved. There is no fee for it, and it covers properties inside the city limits only.

The city's list of examples is:

  • Moving the property into or out of a trust.
  • A divorce, or removing a name.
  • A marriage, or adding a name.
  • A legal name change.
  • A refinance.
  • A foreclosure where the sheriff's deed puts the property in bank ownership. If an individual buys at the sheriff's sale, that buyer purchases a regular stamp.

The exempt packet needs the open account statement, a Certificate for Exemption (mailed and in-person applications only) and a copy of the notarized deed. Anyone moving a house between names ahead of a sale, such as out of a trust or after a divorce, should start with this packet.

sections.h2: Which Naperville permits should a seller check before listing?
sections.html:
Start with any work done after you bought the house. Naperville's permit list includes separate entries for decks, patios and sheds, driveways, fences, generators, lawn sprinkler systems with an RPZ backflow preventer, plumbing, electrical work, swimming pools and residential room additions or alterations.

If you cannot find paperwork for a finished basement, a deck or a sprinkler system, call the city and ask whether a permit was issued for that address. It is easier to learn the answer before a buyer's inspector or attorney raises the question.

If the house has unfinished work you do not want to complete, a buyer paying cash can take it as it stands and handle permits afterward.

sections.h2: How do floods and weather affect a Naperville house sale?
sections.html:
The flood record matters more than the snow. The area took 14 inches of rain in under 24 hours in 1996, DuPage County was declared a disaster area, and damage topped $30 million. A second major flood followed in 2013.

Much of the land along the West Branch of the DuPage River is owned by the Forest Preserve District, which keeps development out of the floodplain and reduces overbank damage. Even so, ask your insurance agent about your parcel before you list, since buyers' lenders will ask the same question about flood zones.

Naperville has a humid continental climate with cold, snowy winters and hot summers. The recorded extremes are 105 degrees Fahrenheit and minus 29. Average precipitation runs about 37.7 inches a year, which makes sump pumps, gutters and grading the items buyers examine first on older homes.

sections.h2: What do Census figures say about Naperville homes and owners?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 figures describe a high-value, owner-heavy market:

  • Owner-occupied rate: 74.8%.
  • Median value of an owner-occupied home: $540,200.
  • Median selected monthly owner costs: $3,154 with a mortgage and $1,305 without.
  • Median gross rent: $1,885.
  • Households: 54,847, at 2.70 persons per household.
  • Median household income: $155,105, and 72.5% of adults 25 and older hold a bachelor's degree or higher.
  • Mean travel time to work: 30.5 minutes.

About 22.5% of residents were born outside the United States, and 26.9% of residents age 5 and older speak a language other than English at home.

sections.h2: Which schools, roads and employers anchor Naperville neighborhoods?
sections.html:
Two school districts cover most of the city. Naperville Community Unit District 203 serves central and northern Naperville and runs Naperville Central and Naperville North high schools. Indian Prairie School District 204 serves much of the rest. Small areas fall in District 200 on the DuPage side, and Plainfield District 202 and Valley View District 365U on the Will side.

Interstate 88, the Reagan Tollway, crosses the north end, and Illinois Route 59 meets it at a diverging diamond interchange that opened in 2015. Ogden Avenue is US 34. Metra and Amtrak both stop in Naperville on the BNSF line.

The city's 2020 financial report, as summarized by Wikipedia, listed Edward Hospital with 4,500 employees, District 204 with 3,071 and Nokia with 2,750 as the largest employers. North Central College, on a 59-acre campus downtown, has been in Naperville since 1870.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Naperville house in its current condition?
faqs.a: Yes, a buyer can agree to take the house as it stands, and that is a term of your contract. The city side of the closing is the transfer stamp packet and the statement of open accounts, and neither of those asks you to make repairs first.

faqs.q: Who pays the Naperville transfer tax stamp?
faqs.a: The buyer does. The city's ordinance requires buyers of residential or commercial property inside incorporated Naperville to purchase the stamp, at the rate of $1.50 per $500 of purchase price printed on the city's page.

faqs.q: How early should I start the Naperville paperwork before closing?
faqs.a: At least seven business days early. The city asks for the Statement of Open Account request no later than seven business days before closing, and stamp processing itself can take up to seven business days.

faqs.q: Does it matter if my Naperville home is on the Will County side?
faqs.a: It changes where the deed is recorded and the fee. Will County parcels record with the Will County Recorder of Deeds, whose standard document fee is $90.00 from October 1, 2025, while DuPage County lists $86.00. The city's own stamp rules are the same on both sides.

faqs.q: Which deed changes in Naperville need an exempt stamp?
faqs.a: Any change of name on a house you already own, such as adding a spouse, removing a name after a divorce, moving the property into a trust or refinancing. A sheriff's deed that puts the property in bank ownership also qualifies, with no fee for the exempt stamp.
